messages.subject: [statnet_help] 4 cycle blues
messages.body_plain:
Greetings statnet cognoscenti,
      I have a series of clarifying/advice seeking questions related to
4-cycles. My apologies if these are largely obvious and/or stupid. For
context, I am currently modeling an undirected bipartite network (i.e., so
that a 4 cycle involves 2 nodes from each mode, and there are no 2 cycles
or 3 cycles).

1. The gwnsp term includes 0 and 1 nsp counts, which are not 4 cycles - is
there currently a means to fit a weighted term that in essence is gwnsp but
does not model 0s and 1s, to avoid having to fit nsp(2) + nsp(3)...?

2. I know the cycle(4) parameter is a direct way to count 4 cycles, but
this term seems to impose a uniquely prohibitive computational burden. I
have a large, 1385 by 2225 bipartite network, which is obviously part of
the problem, but the cycle(4) term hangs even on a high powered simulation
cluster in a way that no other term (gw___, kstar, triangle, etc.) comes
remotely close to. This problem seems directly attributable to the
computation burden of the term (and not an idiosyncratic data issue), as
fitting behavior is similar for simulated networks of a similar size. Are
there any strategies specifically related to modeling high high-ordered
cycle term that might be constructive?

3. In an older post to the usergroup page, Carter Butts discussed setting
an offset parameter for 4 cycles (http://mailman13.u.washington
.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2014/001886.html) as a way to at least make
sure that the model explores a parameter space with an appropriate 4 cycle
density level. Is there a principled way in which I might go about
identifying a suitable offset coefficient, or is that choice largely
ad-hoc?

Thanks for your time.

-tyler


-- 
Tyler Scott
tyler.andrew.scott@gmail.com

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 4 cycle blues
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Tyler -


On 08/01/2017 05:42 PM, Tyler Scott wrote:
> Greetings statnet cognoscenti,
>       I have a series of clarifying/advice seeking questions related 
> to 4-cycles. My apologies if these are largely obvious and/or stupid. 
> For context, I am currently modeling an undirected bipartite network 
> (i.e., so that a 4 cycle involves 2 nodes from each mode, and there 
> are no 2 cycles or 3 cycles).
>
> 1. The gwnsp term includes 0 and 1 nsp counts, which are not 4 cycles 
> - is there currently a means to fit a weighted term that in essence is 
> gwnsp but does not model 0s and 1s, to avoid having to fit nsp(2) + 
> nsp(3)...?
>
If you think that NSP(1) and NSP(0) will behave differently from what 
GWNSP imposes, you could try adding those two terms to the formula; this 
might or might not be unstable, depending on whether the corresponding 
statistics strongly diverge from what would be expected under the 
general geometric weighting pattern (among other things).

> 2. I know the cycle(4) parameter is a direct way to count 4 cycles, 
> but this term seems to impose a uniquely prohibitive computational 
> burden. I have a large, 1385 by 2225 bipartite network, which is 
> obviously part of the problem, but the cycle(4) term hangs even on a 
> high powered simulation cluster in a way that no other term (gw___, 
> kstar, triangle, etc.) comes remotely close to. This problem seems 
> directly attributable to the computation burden of the term (and not 
> an idiosyncratic data issue), as fitting behavior is similar for 
> simulated networks of a similar size. Are there any strategies 
> specifically related to modeling high high-ordered cycle term that 
> might be constructive?

The complexity of counting cycles scales as something like n^L, where L 
is the cycle length and n is the size of the largest "dense" cluster in 
the graph.  (This is a heuristic, hence the scare quotes.)  Not having 
triangles helps, but even so, if you have a bipartite subgraph that is 
close to complete, you will get costs that increase very sharply.  Raw 
cycle terms can work well in networks that are uniformly sparse, but 
they can go from "no problem" to "no way" fast when your network has 
dense regions of appreciable size.  It sounds like your network must be 
relatively dense (or, at least, that it has a such regions), given that 
you are already hitting the wall with L=4.  I do have some code that 
works faster than the current release version, but given the description 
of the regime you are in, that's not going to do the trick.  Cycles, 
like paths and cliques, are inherently expensive to count unless you are 
in the sparse regime.

If you find that you can very quickly count cycles with kcycle.census or 
summary(blah~cycle(4)) but that ergm() bogs down, the issue is probably 
that your model is taking a detour through a part of the graph space 
that is dense enough to cause computational problems.  Since, per the 
above, the transition from fast to slow is very abrupt for cycle terms, 
it is certainly possible to have this happen.  This is challenging to 
work around, but you may be able to make headway by first fitting other 
parts of your model (and ensuring that they do not lead to dense draws), 
and then using the other parameters as seeds for a run that adds the 
cycle term. Essentially, the issue in this case is that the optimization 
procedure thinks it ought to be able to search the parameter space 
however it likes, but some parts of the space are not computationally 
feasible; these parts may indeed be far from the MLE (and hence, in 
principle, irrelevant), but the optimizer doesn't know that.  Coming up 
with smart procedures that try to recognize when they have entered bad 
parts of the parameter space without churning all the way through an 
MCMC run has been informally discussed, but to my knowledge this is 
still an open problem. Regardless, ensuring that you have incorporated 
other elements in your model that will act to inhibit runaway tie 
formation is an important first step.  (What they should be is 
impossible to say without knowing the intimate details of your system, 
your data, the mechanisms that drive it, etc.  But be sure your model 
makes use of any information you have on inhibitors of interaction.)

Given all this, you _could_ also try to deal with "dense detours" by 
imposing degree or other constraints that enforce sparsity (setting them 
well above what is seen in the data, so that hopefully they act only to 
reign in wayward chains).  The intuition is that, so long as the 
constraint is in a certain sense far from the regime in which the data 
lives, it will only get used for parameter values that aren't near the 
MLE anyway, and hence can improve computational performance with little 
or no impact on the final solution.  The risk is that the MCMC really 
will encounter the constraint with non-negligible probability near the 
MLE, in which case your estimates will be biased.  A careful examination 
of the MCMC trace can confirm that this is or is not happening.  I am 
hesitant to recommend this strategy, due to the care that must be 
exercised, but it is among the tricks one can use.  It won't help you if 
the data itself is sufficiently dense for cycle counting to be 
prohibitive, but it can help if the problem is transient in nature.

>
> 3. In an older post to the usergroup page, Carter Butts discussed 
> setting an offset parameter for 4 cycles 
> (http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2014/001886.html 
> <http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2014/001886.html>) 
> as a way to at least make sure that the model explores a parameter 
> space with an appropriate 4 cycle density level. Is there a principled 
> way in which I might go about identifying a suitable offset 
> coefficient, or is that choice largely ad-hoc?
>

What I was suggesting was systematically varying the cycle parameter and 
using simulation to examine the behavior of the model as a function of 
the cycle term.  You would want to pick a range of values, and perform 
the fit->simulate process for each (using it as the value of a cycle(4) 
offset parameter).  Bracketing the range of values is fairly easily done 
by trial and error (when too high, you'll get overproduction of cycles 
relative to the data, and when too low, you'll get underproduction); if 
you need a systematic method, try starting at 0 and exponentially 
searching in both directions.  Once you have bracketed the range of what 
is reasonable, evaluation on an evenly spaced grid is one reasonable 
approach.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

> Thanks for your time.
>
> -tyler
>
>
> -- 
> Tyler Scott
> tyler.andrew.scott@gmail.com <mailto:tyler.andrew.scott@gmail.com>
>

> statnet_help mailing list
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM missing data, interpretation and sample size questions
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] STERGM missing data, interpretation and sample size questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet,



I have a series of clarifying/advice seeking questions related to the TERGM
package for STERGM.  Forgive me if these are rather basic questions in
network analysis. I have read and reread the STERGM manual and just cannot
figure out the answers.



1)      I am starting to work in the TERGM package to run a longitudinal
network analysis with directed networks. The issue is that depending on the
wave of data collection (there are four time points) individuals come and
go from the network so I have some missing data. I know there are ways
through imputation, either forwards, backwards, majority, all as ?0? or ?1?
through the impute.network.list() function. What would be the justification
or rule of thumb for preferring one method over the others?



2)      Another question is that periodically, when running some
simulations and analyzing a STERGM (with the TERGM package), I get -Inf
values for the parameter estimates.  Why is this happening and how is it
interpreted?  For example, I get a -Inf value for the edge term in the
summary of dissolution of the STERGM. Does this mean, when transformed from
log-odds to probability, that the probability of a tie persisting is 0, and
said a different way it means the probability of ties dissolving as 100%?
Is it correct in the dissolution portion to interpret the edge term
estimate as the log-odds of a tie persisting when the estimate is positive
and the log-odds of a tie dissolving if the estimate is negative?  An
example of this is in the code and output below;



seed1 <- sample(1:10000, 1, replace = T)

seed2 <- sample(1:10000, 1, replace = T)

seed3 <- sample(1:10000, 1, replace = T)



g0 <- network(20, density = 0.06, directed = TRUE)



g1 <- simulate(~edges + mutual, nsim = 1,

               coef = c(-2.8172, 0), basis = g0,

               control = control.simulate(MCMC.burnin = 1000,

                                          MCMC.interval = 100), seed = seed1)

g2 <- simulate(~edges + mutual, nsim = 1,

               coef = c(-3.0412, 0), basis = g1,

               control = control.simulate(MCMC.burnin = 1000,

                                          MCMC.interval = 100), seed = seed2)

g3 <- simulate(~edges + mutual, nsim = 1,

               coef = c(-3.562, 0), basis = g2,

               control = control.simulate(MCMC.burnin = 1000,

                                          MCMC.interval = 100), seed = seed2)



g.net <- list()

g.net[[1]] <- g0

g.net[[2]] <- g1

g.net[[3]] <- g2

g.net[[4]] <- g3



st.g.net <- stergm(g.net,

                   formation = ~edges + mutual,

                   dissolution = ~edges + mutual,

                   estimate = "CMLE",

                   control = control.stergm(init.form = NULL,

                                            init.diss = NULL,

                                            init.method = 0,

                                            force.main = FALSE,

                                           SA.restart.on.err = FALSE),

                   times = 1:4)



summary(st.g.net)  # STERGM Results

##

## ==============================

## Summary of formation model fit

## ==============================

##

## Formula:   ~edges + mutual

##

## Iterations:  2 out of 20

##

## Monte Carlo MLE Results:

##        Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value

## edges   -3.3047     0.1730      0  <1e-04 ***

## mutual   1.1008     0.4576      0  0.0163 *

## ---

## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

##

##      Null Deviance: 1501.4  on 1083  degrees of freedom

##  Residual Deviance:  363.1  on 1081  degrees of freedom

##

## AIC: 367.1    BIC: 377.1    (Smaller is better.)

##

## ================================

## Summary of dissolution model fit

## ================================

##

## Formula:   ~edges + mutual

##

## Iterations:  0 out of 20

##

## Monte Carlo MLE Results:

##        Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value

## edges      -Inf          0      0  <1e-04 ***

## mutual     -Inf          0      0  <1e-04 ***

## ---

## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

##

## Log-likelihood was not estimated for this fit.

## To get deviances, AIC, and/or BIC from fit `object$dissolution.fit` run

##   > object$dissolution.fit<-logLik(object$dissolution.fit, add=TRUE)

## to add it to the object or rerun this function with eval.loglik=TRUE.



3)      Lastly, there is a package called BTERGM for TERGM analysis. What
restricts STERGM to require networks at each time point to have the same
number of nodes, while the BTERM package allows for varying numbers of
nodes at each time point?  Is this due to the BTERGM package looking at the
overall edge term, while the STERGM looks specifically at formation and
dissolution separately? If so, would someone be able to help me make sense
of that?





I greatly appreciate any insight on these questions!


Best,

Nate

following terms: b1star(k), b2star(k) and cycle(k). While using, for
example, b2star(k, attrname=NULL), how many values of k should I take?
Is there something like a bipartite gwesp term?

The other question might be related to something going wrong with my
conversion of a networkx (Python) graph to an R igraph graph, but I
cannot figure out what it is. Although my graph g is indeed bipartite
(it passes the test is_bipartite(g)), after I convert it t ao statnet
graph as

g.s <-network::as.network(as.matrix(A), directed=FALSE,biparite=TRUE)

and I run

m03 <- formula(g.s ~ edges + b2star(3, attrname=NULL))
summary.statistics(m03)
m03.ergm <- ergm(m03)
m03.ergm

I get the error

Error in check.ErgmTerm(nw, arglist, directed = FALSE, bipartite =
TRUE, : The ERGM term may not be used with networks with
bipartite==FALSE

I understand that there's something I've missed to do and I would
appreciate your assistance on the above.

Best,

--Moses

messages.subject: [statnet_help] statnet ERGM question
messages.body_plain:
HI,
I have a question regarding the formulation of an ERGM model.
I was wondering a) how do you test for multi-collinearity?
                My model is producing NAs in the output (however, it does not do this if I take out another term) and I was wondering if this is due to multi-collinearity.
                                b) Is there a rule regarding the number of terms in the model formulation equation with respect to over fitting the model?
                                i.e. my model looks like this:
m1=ergm(new1~edges +
                   nodematch('pasture')+ nodematch('sex')+nodematch('breed')+nodematch('use')+
                   nodecov('age')+
                   nodefactor('pasture')+ nodefactor('sex')+nodefactor('breed')+nodefactor('use')
        )
                My network consists of 28 nodes, 225 edges and has a density of .595 . The model output says I have 378 degrees of freedom. Am I including too many terms for my data? How would I calculate the appropriate number of dof for my data?

Thanks in advance,
Rachael Milwid
PhD (c), University of Guelph
